message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
Working from memory as the request asks, here is what I recall. Wording will be approximate in places, and I've flagged where I'm unsure.

**Opening**
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight.
- Part of that weight comes from evidence, part from the track record of whoever stands behind it, and experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have usually been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, reflecting checks they've already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly, but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected; understating is "more insidious".
- A newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work done well.
- **Example:** a colleague reports a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If they've managed that supplier for years, take the report as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding, make sure you've taken the material in, and show it: restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This is not politeness; it's how a conversation moves forward rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement puts people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; the useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, pick up the points you can act on now, and note that the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- A shared record lets the team build together. Members insisting on their own readings fragment the team into "private versions of the truth", and it stops being able to act.
- **Example:** team notes say a report shows "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles, some it leaves uncertain; mark which is which and keep the work moving.
- An open question has a cost: it blocks dependent decisions, invites repeated discussion, and leaves colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. It can be revisited if something new comes up; a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safer, is the more common one in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save energy for live questions.
- **Example:** a trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow; handle problems there as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see material differently. That can be valuable, but only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- When asking someone to check your work, brief them: what you've concluded, where you see risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- When you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the timing is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time; take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- You'll often see a good next step; before taking it, check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once you've confirmed the direction, and release the result when it's ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked, costing more than a short conversation would have.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your position; the owner sees considerations you can't, and asking is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps need no sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first and act together.
- **Example:** rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other; know both sides.
- The six pairs:
  - **Overclaiming / second-guessing:** overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
  - **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous; missing one that is.
  - **Closing too early / keeping open too long:** declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the team's answer.
  - **Abandoning a line / relitigating one:** dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening a decided one.
  - **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively:** accepting anything; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
  - **Acting alone / waiting too long:** making calls others should have shaped; delaying agreed steps.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- This isn't a rulebook to consult at every step; it describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, a direction everyone has agreed.
- Trust those; they are how good work gets done together.

**Where I'm least confident**
- The exact order of the pairs in §7, and the precise wording of each pair label.
- Whether the "private versions of the truth" phrasing is verbatim.
- The exact wording of the §6 sequence (drafts, call, release).
